evidence.quote: This study recruited a total of 24 stroke patients from Tianjin Huanhu Hospital, including 18 males and 6 females. The patients ranged in age from 34 to 77 years, with a mean age of 55.75 years. Among them, 15 had right hemiplegia and 9 had left hemiplegia. And fourteen patients received brain-computer interface (BCI) training (BCI group), while 10 patients received conventional physical rehabilitation therapy (Traditional group). The BCI training involved a 2-week rehabilitation program using the brain-controlled “sixth-finger”15,17 system independently developed by the research team from Tianjin University. The conventional physical training consisted of a 2-week rehabilitation program and administered by rehabilitation physicians from Tianjin Huanhu Hospital. The BCI group and traditional group received equivalent training dosages. Each intervention consisted of 8 training sessions over 2 weeks, with 4 sessions per week, and each session lasted approximately 45 min. In addition, all patients underwent three functional assessments: immediately before the intervention (pre-training), immediately after the intervention (post-training), and 1 month after the intervention (follow-up).

Patient eligibility was assessed by medical professionals, and the inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) aged 30–80 years; (2) first-ever stroke due to cerebral hemorrhage or infarction; (3) disease duration of 3–14 months; and (4) normal cognitive function, and ability to comprehend and perform experimental tasks. Exclusion criteria included: (1) severe psychological disorders or epilepsy that could interfere with task completion, and (2) scalp conditions preventing valid EEG acquisition. The dataset includes three collection phases: the pre-training phase, collected before patients undergo a two-week training period; the post-training phase, collected immediately after patients complete the two-week training; and the follow-up phase, collected after a one-month washout period following the completion of the training. 19/24 patients participated in all EEG data collection phases, while 5/24 patients were absent from the follow-up data collection due to personal reasons. Our dataset is available in the Figshare repository21, is organized as Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS)22, a widely adopted format for open EEG datasets, facilitating straightforward access and reuse. The dataset structure is illustrated in Fig. 2. The repository is divided into four main sections: (1) Raw data, containing the original EEG recordings for each subject throughout the entire experiment, stored as ‘.set/.fdt’ files; (2) Preprocessed data, stored as ‘.mat’ files; (3) Additional information, including patient details, electrode locations, and EEG event markers; and (4) Code, provided as MATLAB scripts.Fig. 2The EEG dataset structure.

This section includes the unprocessed, unsegmented EEG data recorded for each patient throughout the entire experiment. The ‘.set’ and ‘.fdt’ files store meta information and raw data respectively. These files can be loaded using the EEGLAB plugin to obtain an ‘EEG’ structure variable, which contains the raw data formatted as ‘channels × time-samples’, channel information, sampling rate, label information, etc. The naming convention is consistent with that of the preprocessed data, as shown below:\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${sub}-{xx}{\rm{\_}}{group}{\rm{\_}}s{ession}{\rm{\_}}{yy}{\rm{\_}}{original}.{set}/.{fdt}$$\end{document}sub−xx_group_session_yy_original.set/.fdtwhere ‘xx’ is the subject ID, ‘group’ is the intervention group received for patients (B represents BCI group, T represents Traditional group), ‘session’ indicates the collection phases (pre represents the pre-training phase, post represents the post-training phase, follow represents the follow-up phase), and ‘yy’ is the run number.

Raw data were preprocessed using the EEGLAB toolbox based on MATLAB and saved in ‘.mat’ format. These files can be loaded directly through MATLAB to obtain an ‘EEG’ structure that contains the preprocessed data and meta information. In this study, each trial of the SF-MI and AH-MI tasks lasted 6 s. Based on the earlier finding that the ERD phenomenon tends to stabilize after 0.5~1 s, the EEG data segment from 1 s~5 s after the onset of the MI task was selected for classification. The extracted 4 s data segment from each trial was treated as an independent sample, thereby ensuring trial-level independence and preventing overly optimistic classification performance caused by temporal adjacency between samples. And other researchers may adopt customized sample-segmentation strategies according to their specific research objectives and analytical requirements. To demonstrate the inherent classifiability induced by the MI paradigm itself, this study employed classical machine learning algorithms for the binary classification task between SF-MI and AH-MI. EEG features were extracted using the Common Spatial Pattern (CSP) method, and the resulting feature vectors were subsequently classified using both support vector machine (SVM) and linear discriminant analysis (LDA) classifiers. A 10-fold cross-validation procedure was applied, in which the EEG data of each subject was randomly partitioned into 10 groups. For each fold, one group was used as the test set and the remaining nine groups as the training set. This process was repeated 10 times, and the average of the results was taken as the classification accuracy for each subject. The final classification accuracy was then computed as the mean across all subjects.
